planting.note: Divide congested rhizome clumps in spring as new growth resumes, ensuring each division keeps healthy roots attached.

directions: Dottie is among the most dramatically colored of the roseopicta cultivars, with near-black, deep olive-green leaves overlaid by a bold, continuous band of hot pink just inside the leaf margin and fine pink feathering along the midrib, set off by wine-purple undersides. The near-black background gives the pink far more contrast than the softer pastel banding of 'Medallion' or the concentric rose-and-silver halo of 'Corona', making Dottie easy to tell apart from its roseopicta relatives at a glance. It wants bright, indirect light since direct sun quickly fades the dark pigmentation, along with consistently moist, humus-rich soil and humidity above 50 percent to prevent crisping leaf edges. Like other roseopicta forms it reacts poorly to tap water minerals, so water with rainwater or water left open overnight, and divide crowded rhizome clumps in spring.

planting.note: Divide the rhizome clump in spring once new growth resumes, keeping several growing points per division.

directions: Rosy carries a softer, more understated pattern than its roseopicta relatives, with silvery sage-green leaves brushed by a diffuse wash of dusty pink radiating from the midrib rather than the crisp banding of 'Medallion' or the near-black ground of 'Dottie'. The muted, powdery coloring gives established clumps a frosted look that reads more subtly in mixed shade plantings, though the leaves still perform the same nightly upward fold and morning release typical of the genus. Grow in bright indirect to medium shade with steady warmth, high humidity, and evenly moist, fast-draining, peat-rich soil, since low humidity or hard tap water quickly shows up as brown, crispy leaf margins. Propagate by dividing the rhizome in spring as new growth resumes.

planting.note: Divide congested clumps in spring; this species is the wild parent of the 'Argentea' and 'Vandenheckei' cultivars and divides the same way.

directions: Goeppertia picturata is the wild-type species behind popular cultivars like 'Argentea' and 'Vandenheckei', with broad, dark green leaves marked by a lighter, silvery-green feathered stripe running from base to tip along the midrib, and undersides in a deep purplish maroon. Compared to the near-solid silver blades of 'Argentea', the species form keeps noticeably more dark green pigment at the leaf margins, giving it a more contrasted, two-toned look. It needs deep to bright indirect shade, warm steady temperatures, and a light, humus-rich mix kept uniformly moist but never waterlogged, with humidity above 55 percent to keep the thin leaf tips from browning. As with its cultivated offspring, water with rainwater or distilled water rather than tap water, and divide congested clumps in spring.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Divide the rhizome clump in spring to propagate or to control size; this species is the wild parent of the 'Medallion' cultivar.

directions: Goeppertia veitchiana is a robust Peruvian rainforest species and the wild parent of the popular 'Medallion' cultivar, producing broad, rounded leaves banded in alternating zones of dark and light green that fan outward from the midrib in a looser, more irregular pattern than the crisp concentric rings bred into 'Medallion'. Mature clumps form an imposing mass of foliage that reads as bolder and coarser-textured than most roseopicta forms, making it a strong solo specimen in a shaded grouping. Provide bright indirect to medium shade, evenly moist and humus-rich soil, and humidity well above 50 percent, since direct sun bleaches the pattern and dry air browns the leaf edges quickly. Divide the rhizome clumps in spring to propagate or to control size.

planting.note: Divide congested clumps in spring as new growth begins; this species is the wild parent of the 'Network' cultivar.

directions: Goeppertia musaica is the species behind the 'Network' cultivar, displaying the same fine, closely spaced grid of intersecting light and dark green lines across the leaf surface, though the wild-type pattern runs slightly looser and less uniform than the tightly geometric mosaic bred into 'Network'. The intricate checkerboard veining is unlike the blotched or banded markings of most other calatheas, giving it strong textural contrast when paired with bolder-patterned prayer plants. It prefers deep shade to bright indirect light, consistently moist and humus-rich soil, and humidity above 50 percent, with tap water minerals reliably causing brown leaf-edge scorch over time. Divide congested clumps in spring as new growth begins to propagate.

planting.note: Divide the rhizome clump in spring, replanting divisions promptly so roots do not dry out.

directions: Goeppertia bachemiana is a lesser-grown but distinctive species with narrow, lance-shaped, pale sage-green leaves marked by a feathered dark green stripe along the midrib and a deep maroon-purple reverse, giving it a more slender, grass-like silhouette than the broad, rounded leaves of roseopicta or veitchiana cultivars. The pale, almost silvery ground color combined with narrow leaf form makes it easy to distinguish from 'Argentea' or 'White Fusion', which carry similar pale tones on much broader foliage. Grow in bright indirect to medium shade with warm, stable temperatures, evenly moist and well-drained humus-rich soil, and humidity above 50 percent to prevent tip browning. Propagate by dividing the rhizome clump in spring.
